forces: Contralto and tenor soloists, mixed chorus, organ and orchestra
performers: Oralia Domínguez, contralto; Raymond Amade, tenor; J. J. Grunenwald, organ; Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
question: When the music becomes quieter, does the prayer become less urgent—or simply more personal?
intro: A dark orchestral prelude opens into a long exchange between chorus, contralto and, later, tenor. Boulanger keeps changing the scale of the plea: massed voices give way to chamber-like detail, then gather strength again. This is the complete psalm on one LP side, not an excerpt from a five-movement work.

cues.title: Depth before the voices
cues.text: The opening works upwards from low sound: organ, drum resonance and lower strings, then a tuba line doubled by solo cello. The choir waits. Listen to the weight of the bass before expecting the melody to occupy the top of the texture.

Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An early withdrawal
cues.text: The first weighty gesture gives way to a much quieter space. Keep the low opening in memory: the prelude is already organised through contrasts, not one uninterrupted crescendo.

cues.title: The upper register opens
cues.text: The prelude also contains a very different kind of writing: a high violin line above the low foundation. Listen for that change of register as a change of perspective, not as the arrival of the chorus.

cues.title: A prize opened Rome
cues.text: In 1913 Boulanger became the first woman to win the Prix de Rome for composition, with Faust et Hélène. The prize brought her to the Villa Medici, where work on this psalm began in 1914.
cues.evidence: Library of Congress biography; psalm chronology: https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1001.html https://guides.loc.gov/feminism-french-women-history/famous/lili-boulanger

cues.title: In memory of her father
cues.text: The psalm is dedicated to the memory of Boulanger’s father, Ernest, who died in 1900. That dedication is documented; it does not require every low note or dissonance to stand for a particular biographical event.
cues.evidence: Dedication and composition history; also the original Everest insert: https://i.discogs.com/XrNcaeuOsiqmWirxmPgDAtlexW1ImUbc9UpE5Aw4kkg/rs:fit/g:sm/q:90/h:600/w:592/czM6Ly9kaXNjb2dz/LWRhdGFiYXNlLWlt/YWdlcy9SLTYwNTY4/NTItMTQ3MzM1MDk5/Ny02MDQ1LmpwZWc.jpeg https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1001.html

cues.title: Together and in overlap
cues.text: Across the choral writing, Boulanger alternates united declamation with lines that overlap. Listen for whether the voices seem to speak together or to continue one another’s thought; that distinction can be clearer than following every chord.

cues.title: Work during the war
cues.text: During the First World War, Lili and Nadia organised support for musicians through the Comité Franco-Américain du Conservatoire. This is part of the work’s historical setting, not evidence that a particular orchestral gesture depicts a battle.
cues.evidence: Library of Congress account of the sisters’ wartime work. https://guides.loc.gov/feminism-french-women-history/famous/lili-boulanger

cues.title: Finished at Gargenville
cues.text: The final page names Rome and Gargenville and dates the work 1914–1917. The score therefore records a multi-year composition, not a single last-minute outpouring. Boulanger completed it before the final months of her life.
cues.evidence: Printed p. 90: Rome–Gargenville, 1914–1917. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP393069-PMLP430943-N0856389_PDF_1_-1DM.pdf

cues.text: Igor Markevitch conducts the Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux and the Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur. Nadia Boulanger’s separate credit is recording supervision. The session location is given as the Salle Pleyel, Paris; the sources consulted do not establish its date.

cues.title: The score outlived its composer
cues.text: Boulanger died in 1918. The consulted orchestral score was published by Durand in 1925, so its printed circulation belongs to the work’s posthumous life. A publication date should not be confused with the 1914–17 dates of composition.
cues.evidence: Durand 1925 edition and plate 10543; biographical dates: https://guides.loc.gov/feminism-french-women-history/famous/lili-boulanger https://imslp.org/wiki/Psaume_CXXX_(Boulanger,_Lili)

transitions.title: The low orchestra makes room for words
transitions.how: The orchestral prelude broadens and diminishes before figure 4, “Tempo lent.” Low instrumental lines and organ resonance remain as the choir enters quietly, with a narrow declamatory shape. The voices therefore emerge from the prelude’s low foundation rather than replacing it with a fresh fanfare. Reduced orchestral pressure makes the words audible without breaking the continuity.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 10–12, figure 4: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP393069-PMLP430943-N0856389_PDF_1_-1DM.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-130.txt: the prelude falls to −15.6 dB by 3:40; a strong change at 3:44 and subsequent increase anchor the choral region. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: The choral mass becomes an individual plea
transitions.how: After the broad choral climax, the score reduces the choir to a few sustained voices and withdraws much of the brass. At figure 12, solo contralto begins over small clarinet figures, harp, organ and restrained strings. The continuing accompaniment holds the connection while the vocal scale changes from collective declamation to a single singer.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 35–38, figures 11 bis–12: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP393069-PMLP430943-N0856389_PDF_1_-1DM.pdf. transitions.title: Running figures survive the collapse in weight
transitions.how: The renewed vocal and orchestral force gives way to Modéré and a chamber-like instrumental passage. Harps and organ retain running figures while flute, solo viola and solo cello pass quieter lines between them. Muted strings and sustained wind notes replace the preceding massed attack. Continuity lies in the accompaniment’s movement, even as the number of foreground voices contracts.

transitions.title: The plea passes from one singer to another
transitions.how: A renewed choral rise diminishes before figure 19, “Sans lenteur.” Contralto and tenor take up the line in imitation, supported by flute figures, harp and a moving organ part. The voices do not simply sing in unison: the second entry extends a thought already under way. A lighter texture allows the continuing motion to remain audible after the larger crest.

transitions.title: The quieter line gathers active companions
transitions.how: The later choral expansion subsides before figure 22’s Allegro. Detached wind and string figures then set the accompaniment moving again around the lower choral voices. Acceleration and crescendo bring more of the ensemble into the renewed declaration. Boulanger reconnects the intimate prayer to public force through rhythmic activity and accumulating orchestral weight.

transitions.title: The final surge returns to low weight
transitions.how: The active final gathering yields to a quieter closing texture. Sustained voices, organ and lower instrumental lines replace the running figures; harp and celesta colour the remaining motion. The end progressively slows and keeps small swells within its restrained dynamics. Low sonority recalls the opening world without supplying a simple triumphant answer to it.

composer.epithet: Her songs and psalms give a sustained bass, a repeated interval and the weight of a choral unison the force of a large formal argument.
facts: Daughter of Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger; younger sister of the composer, conductor and teacher Nadia Boulanger
Paris Conservatoire; composition with Paul Vidal, with extensive musical support from Nadia
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome for musical composition, 1913
Songs, choral works, orchestral and chamber pieces; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
Lili Boulanger grew up in a Paris household where composition, singing and teaching were family work. Her father Ernest had won the Prix de Rome in 1835 and taught singing at the Conservatoire; her mother Raïssa had been his pupil. Nadia, born in 1887, was already receiving serious musical training when Lili was small. Lili learned piano and several other instruments and accompanied her sister into Conservatoire classes. Recurrent illness interrupted her education from childhood. The resulting timetable was irregular, but the musical environment was exceptionally well supplied with teachers, performers and scores.

Nadia was an early mentor and practical support; Lili’s formal composition teacher at the Conservatoire was Paul Vidal. Their training included fugue, harmony and the cantata, extending well beyond the short piano pieces through which women composers were often permitted a public identity. In 1912 illness forced Lili to withdraw from the final stage of the Prix de Rome. She returned in 1913 and won the Premier Grand Prix with Faust et Hélène, becoming the first woman to receive that composition prize. She was nineteen. Nadia had won a second prize in 1908.
